title: Debunking Relevance as the Key to Student Motivation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart pushes back on the popular claim that relevance is the master key to student motivation, arguing the "relevance as king" framing undermines students in three specific ways. First, it discounts cognitive science showing that domain knowledge, not perceived relevance, is what enables comprehension and problem-solving, so skipping "irrelevant" content compounds into later struggle. Second, it implies expertise can be shortcut by teaching students to generically "think like" a historian or scientist, when real expertise requires the long, often-inflexible accumulation of specific domain knowledge. Third, and most provocatively, he links an overemphasis on relevance to moral disengagement, arguing that teaching students their learning must suit their own tastes and identity discourages them from grappling with perspectives, histories, and knowledge outside their own experience. He closes by affirming relevance still has real value as a motivational hook, but argues for a broader, evidence-based framework over any single silver-bullet explanation of motivation.
points: Stuart's central claim: an overemphasis on relevance undermines intellectual potential, since cognitive science shows domain knowledge — not perceived relevance — drives comprehension and transfer.

He argues expertise has no shortcut: teaching students to generically "think like a historian" doesn't substitute for the long accumulation of inflexible domain knowledge that real expertise requires.

His sharpest claim links relevance-mania to moral disengagement — telling students their learning must suit their own tastes and identity discourages them from engaging with people and ideas unlike themselves.
He proposes a broad, culturally rich, coherent K-12 curriculum (echoing David Didau) as the alternative to curricular decisions driven by guesses about what's presently relevant.
quotes: Here's the thing: an overemphasis on relevance undermines our students' intellects, their mastery of our disciplines, and their ability to morally engage with people who are different from them.

Cognitive science has been settled, at least since I began my career, on the evidence-rich idea that the more a person knows in a given domain, the easier it is for that person to solve problems, think critically, comprehend texts, comprehend speech, and learn more things in the given domain.

The path to expert-level thinking is a path through lots of initially inflexible things — things that don't have broad application. This is a somewhat annoying reality of being a human creature v. some kind of demigod.
Third, when we teach our students that they deserve to only be taught what's relevant to them, we also teach them that moral disengagement is an acceptable way to live.
The flourishing life just does seem to depend on learning things — lots of things — in childhood that may not be immediately relevant at the time of learning them.

I'm just saying relevance can't be king. Overemphasizing it will undermine our students' long-term flourishing outcomes because it'll minimize their access to knowledge of the world that is broader than their experience.
